div.p: In the finite element method, we define a function f(x) that can be evaluated anywhere from values at vertices.

div.p: We define f(x) as the weighted sum of three continuous basis functions:

div.p: The basis functions are barycentric coordinates for the point.

div.p: f(x) = fᵢ ɸᵢ(x) + fⱼ ɸⱼ(x) + fₖ ɸₖ(x) = ∑ fᵢ ɸᵢ(x)

div.p: The Laplace operator at a vertex is defined as the divergence of the gradient at that vertex.

div.p: We can express that by looking at a tiny area around the vertex (all incident triangles).

p.style: box-sizing: border-box; color: rgb(29, 29, 29); margin-block: 0px; margin-bottom: 0px; margin-top: 0px; min-block-size: 32px; min-height: 32px; text-rendering: optimizelegibility; unicode-bidi: isolate;

div.p: Each basis function is piecewise linear in a triangle (a piece of plane), which means its gradient is piecewise constant.

p.style: box-sizing: border-box; color: rgb(29, 29, 29); margin-block: 0px; margin-bottom: 0px; margin-top: 0px; min-block-size: 32px; min-height: 32px; text-rendering: optimizelegibility; unicode-bidi: isolate;

div.p: The gradient points in the direction of steepest ascent, which is to say, towards its vertex and perpendicular to the opposite edge.

p.style: box-sizing: border-box; color: rgb(29, 29, 29); margin-block: 0px; margin-bottom: 0px; margin-top: 0px; min-block-size: 32px; min-height: 32px; text-rendering: optimizelegibility; unicode-bidi: isolate;

div.p: The magnitude of the gradient is based on the geometry of the triangle: rise/run.

p.style: box-sizing: border-box; color: rgb(29, 29, 29); margin-block: 0px; margin-bottom: 0px; margin-top: 0px; min-block-size: 32px; min-height: 32px; text-rendering: optimizelegibility; unicode-bidi: isolate;

div.p: It's a basis function, so the rise from the opposite edge vⱼvₖ to vᵢ is 1.

p.style: box-sizing: border-box; color: rgb(29, 29, 29); margin-block: 0px; margin-bottom: 0px; margin-top: 0px; min-block-size: 32px; min-height: 32px; text-rendering: optimizelegibility; unicode-bidi: isolate;

div.p: The run is the height hᵢ.

div.p: That's it! Iterate over every triangle in your mesh and contribute the fᵢ, fⱼ, and fₖ coefficients.

div.p: Don't compute cotangent with trigonometric functions like sine and cosine.

div.p: Using ɸᵢ(x) = 1 - ɸⱼ(x) - ɸₖ(x) and ∇ɸᵢ(x) = - ∇ɸⱼ(x) - ∇ɸₖ(x), we can substitute for fᵢ's coefficient in our original integral and write:

div.p: One final note: We computed the integral of the Laplacian in the entire one-ring, whose area is ∑_(triangles ijk in one-ring of vertex i) A_ijk. To compute a point-wise Laplacian at the vertex, divide by ∑ A_ijk. If you use this Laplacian to compute the integrated Laplacian over the mesh, we would then re-scale each vertex Laplacian by a "mass" or area that partitions the mesh. For this, the Barycentric or Voronoi area for a vertex is often used. The Barycentric area is particularly easy to compute: A_barycentric = A_ijk/3. Putting that together, we could pre-scale our weights by:

div.p: We could have equivalently computed the integral in the area obtained by connecting the midpoints of the edges ij and ik. The gradient is constant in the triangle. Via medial triangle identities, the outward facing normal is the same, too. Side lengths are exactly halved. So our original integral:
